Piker was at El-Sayed’s primary election night party and even spoke to the cameras after El-Sayed won.

   “Changes are coming,” he said.

   Is this who the new Democratic Party is becoming? Some readers will tear their hair out with that question, but that’s what many voters are now asking. And it’s a question Republicans are hoping will continue to be asked.

   Which raises the question: What is November about?

   There’s a new, energetic, extremely progressive crop of Democratic candidates on ballots across the country. While this has excited a number of Democratic primary voters, it has unnerved many others. If Republicans can use figures like Piker to stir more angst among Democrats and potentially drive more motivation among GOP voters, it could tip the balance in a race or two. Do Democrats Have a Hasan Piker Problem?
 
Plus, the Postal Service faces mail-ballot allegations, and the U.S. renews strikes on Iran
 
 
JULIA DEMAREE NIKHINSON/AP
 

Good morning. Hasan Piker, an online streamer and unapologetic provocateur, has emerged as a polarizing figure in this 2026 election cycle. He is forcing Democrats to wrestle with a very uncomfortable question: How fringe are they willing to become?

 

Piker has said controversial things that have been well-documented about Sept. 11 and American Jews, among other things. Many Democrats try to wave him away. But he’s not a nobody. He has campaigned with Abdul El-Sayed, a bit of a provocateur himself who also happens to be the Democrats’ candidate for Senate in Michigan. Piker was at El-Sayed’s primary election night party and even spoke to the cameras after El-Sayed won.

 

“Changes are coming,” he said.

 

Is this who the new Democratic Party is becoming? Some readers will tear their hair out with that question, but that’s what many voters are now asking. And it’s a question Republicans are hoping will continue to be asked.

 

“He was attached to your hip during the primary,” Rep. Lisa McClain (R., Mich.) said of El-Sayed and Piker late last month. She added: “Hasan Piker is who the Democrats are.”

 

Democrats are screaming left and right (OK, mostly left) that this is all just a GOP attempt to create distractions from the real issues that matter to voters.

 

“I’m done,” Rep. Debbie Dingell (D., Mich.) told voters recently. “This election is about what’s going to happen when we elect Abdul to the United States Senate. I am done so don’t any reporter ask me again about Hasan Piker. It’s not what November is about.”

 

Which raises the question: What is November about?

 

There’s a new, energetic, extremely progressive crop of Democratic candidates on ballots across the country. While this has excited a number of Democratic primary voters, it has unnerved many others. If Republicans can use figures like Piker to stir more angst among Democrats and potentially drive more motivation among GOP voters, it could tip the balance in a race or two. And that’s all it might take.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Ed Markey: The 80-year-old Democratic senator from Massachusetts trounced Rep. Seth Moulton in the party’s state primary.

 

Hung Cao: Trump is nominating the veteran for Navy secretary, a job that has been vacant since spring.

 

Kirk Trial: The man accused of killing Charlie Kirk potentially faces the death penalty after a Utah judge ruled there was enough evidence to warrant a trial for aggravated murder.

 

President Trump’s Wednesday: Trump has policy meetings this morning, then will meet with travel executives in the afternoon before a Rose Garden dinner this evening.

What I’m Following

 
 
WILLIAM LIANG/ASSOCIATED PRESS
 

The Postal Service has come under fire over mail-in ballots. A whistleblower alleged the Postal Service rushed through new mail-in ballot regulations and is ill-equipped to carry them out for the midterms. This comes as multiple courts consider arguments about whether the USPS has legal authority to implement the regulations at all.

 

The U.S. launched a fresh wave of attacks on Iran. The U.S. carried out new strikes on Iranian targets Tuesday, as Trump said the operation was launched in retaliation for Tehran’s attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks targeting American servicemembers in the Middle East. There has been an uptick of exchanges in recent days, as both sides fight to control the Strait of Hormuz.

 

Republicans hope to rake in cash at the GOP’s midterm convention. The Republican National Committee has planned a pair of high-dollar fundraisers during this month’s convention in Dallas. A roundtable with Trump will cost $250,000 a person to attend, and a photo with the president will be $88,600.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• A Thai resort is hosting the USS Abraham Lincoln after its grueling eight-month deployment.

 

• Bond yields rose to their highest level in years, defying efforts by governments to calm investor fears about mountains of debt and stubborn inflation.

 

• In a surprise twist, California lawmakers failed to pass a watered-down wildfire bill.

 

• Apple updated its Maps application to show Lake America, following Google’s decision to do the same after Trump renamed the lake in an executive order last week.

 

• The House overwhelmingly passed a bipartisan resolution to fund the government past a Sept. 30 deadline.
